speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. I see you are a newborn presenting with respiratory distress; how long has this difficulty breathing been occurring, and was there a prolonged rupture of membranes or any fever during pregnancy?

speaker: Patient
text: Newborn, born after the 32nd gestational week. The baby was born via cesarean delivery. The mother had gestational diabetes but was otherwise healthy with no other pregnancy-related diseases.

speaker: Doctor
text: That is concerning; premature birth and maternal gestational diabetes are significant risk factors. Did the baby require immediate resuscitation or ventilation upon arrival, and are you noticing any specific signs like grunting, nasal flaring, or chest retractions?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Respiratory distress. I also have Tachypnea, Subcostal and intercostal retractions, Nasal flaring, Cyanosis.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS).

The clinical picture of a premature infant (born at 32 weeks) presenting with tachypnea, grunting, nasal flaring, and severe retractions is classic for RDS due to surfactant deficiency. I will confirm this with an Arterial_Blood_Gas and a Chest_X-Ray to visualize the air bronchogram.
